artists.biography:
Talking Heads was an American New Wave and avant-garde band formed in 1975 in New York City and active until 1991. The band comprised David Byrne, Chris Frantz, Tina Weymouth and Jerry Harrison. Auxiliary musicians also regularly made appearances in concert and on the group's albums. The New Wave style of Talking Heads combined elements of punk, art rock, avant-garde, pop, funk, world music, and Americana. Frontman and songwriter David Byrne contributed whimsical, esoteric lyrics to the band's songs, and emphasized their showmanship through various multimedia projects and performances.
Critic Stephen Thomas Erlewine describes Talking Heads as being "one of the most critically acclaimed bands of the '80s, while managing to earn several pop hits." In 2002, the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Four of the band's albums appeared on Rolling Stone magazine's 2003 list of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time, and the Channel 4 100 Greatest Albums poll listed one album (Fear of Music) at number 76. On a 2011 update of Rolling Stone's "100 Greatest Artists of All Time", the band was ranked at #100.

The Name of This Band Is Talking Heads, released in 1982 on Sire Records, is a double live album that captures the evolution of Talking Heads’ sound and stage presence across several pivotal years. The first disc features the original quartet—David Byrne, Chris Frantz, Tina Weymouth, and Jerry Harrison—performing energetic new wave and art rock tracks from their early albums, including Talking Heads: 77, More Songs About Buildings and Food, and Fear of Music. These recordings, drawn from shows in 1977 and 1979, highlight the band’s minimalist, angular style and Byrne’s distinctive vocals.

The second disc showcases the expanded ten-piece lineup that toured in 1980 and 1981, reflecting the group’s embrace of funk, African rhythms, and layered instrumentation heard on Remain in Light. With additional musicians like Adrian Belew, Bernie Worrell, and Nona Hendryx, the performances are more complex and rhythmically dense, illustrating the band’s adventurous approach to live music. The album serves as a bridge between Talking Heads’ early punk-influenced sound and their later, more experimental phase, offering fans a comprehensive look at their artistic growth.

Critically, The Name of This Band Is Talking Heads was praised for its dynamic range and the clarity of its live recordings, capturing the band’s reputation as an innovative and compelling live act. While not a commercial blockbuster, it solidified Talking Heads’ status as one of the most important and influential rock bands of the era, and remains a key document of their live prowess and musical evolution.
